en: Oṃ! O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious;
may we, with steady limbs and bodies, praise [you] with joyful hearts.
May we attain the life-span ordained by the gods. May Indra, of far-reaching fame, grant us well-being;
may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, whose wheel is unbroken, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!
The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: "What is Sītā? What is her form? ||1||
Prajāpati said: "She is Sītā, she is Sītā. Because she is the form of the primordial material cause (mūlaprakṛti), she is remembered as Prakṛti;
because she is the form of the primordial material cause of the Praṇava, she is called Prakṛti. ||2||
Sītā, whose nature consists of the three letters, is Māyā herself in manifest form; Viṣṇu, the seed of the phenomenal world, is called Māyā by the letter *ī*. (3)
The letter *sa* is proclaimed as truth, immortality, attainment, and Soma;
the letter *ta* is remembered as the lofty glory (*tāralakṣmī*), Vairāja, and the sacrificial grass (*prastara*). ||4||
Soma, in the form of the vowel *ī*, adorned with divine ornaments such as garlands and pearls consisting of the particles of nectar, Mahāmāyā—whose nature is unmanifest—becomes manifest. ||5||
The first [form] consists of the Śabdabrahman and is serene during the time of Vedic study;
the second, possessing a manifesting nature, arose upon the earth at the tip of a plow.
The third has the form of the syllable *ī* and is of unmanifest nature; thus they declare her to be Sītā in the tradition of Śaunaka. (6)
By virtue of the proximity of Śrī Rāma, she brings joy to the world;
she is the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of all embodied beings. (7)
The blessed Sītā is to be known as that which is designated as Mūlaprakṛti (the Root Nature);
for the exponents of Brahman say that she is Prakṛti because of her being the Praṇava. ||8||
And also: "Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. (1.1.1)

She is composed of all the Vedas, composed of all the gods, composed of all the worlds, composed of all fame, composed of all dharmas, and composed of the cause and effect that support everything; she is Mahālakṣmī, whose form is both distinct and non-distinct from the Lord of Gods, whose nature is both conscious and unconscious, whose essence is Brahman and the immobile world, who takes the form of bodies according to the distinctions of their qualities, actions, and divisions—appearing in the forms of gods, sages, humans, and gandharvas, and appearing in the forms of the bodies of asuras, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other elemental beings, and is likewise known to be the form of the elements, the senses, the mind, and the vital breaths. ||10||
That Goddess is threefold: she who has Śakti as her seat, the power of will (icchā-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the manifest power (sākṣāt-śakti). ||11||
The power of will (icchā-śakti) becomes threefold:
it consists of Śrī, Bhūmi, and Nīlā; it has the form of Bhadrā; it has the form of radiance; and it takes the form of the moon, sun, and fire. ||12||

She exists as the essence of the *soma* plant among herbs; she manifests as the flowers, fruits, creepers, and shrubs of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*); she consists of medicinal plants and remedies, and takes the form of nectar for the gods, bestowing the fruit of the great soma-sacrifices (*mahastoma*). She produces satisfaction for the gods through nectar, for animals through food, and for all various living beings through grass.

Illuminating all worlds, beginning with the sun, she is both day and night; manifesting through the divisions of time starting from the smallest unit of *nimeṣa* up to *ghaṭikā*, *yāma*, day, week, night, fortnight, month, season, solstice, and year—and by the human convention of a hundred-year lifespan—she appears as "long" or "short. Revolving like a wheel in the manner of the "wheel of time" (*kālacakra*) and the "wheel of the world" (*jagaccakra*), starting from a *nimeṣa* up to the highest number, *parārdha*, these specific divisions of this very Time, which are of the nature of light, become the forms of Time itself. (14)

Agni takes the form of hunger and thirst for living beings such as those who consume food and drink; it is the mouth of the gods; it is the form of cold and heat for forest plants; and it exists within and without wood as both the eternal and the non-eternal. ||15||

The Goddess Śrī, having assumed a threefold form, maintains her manifestation for the sake of protecting the world in accordance with the will of the Blessed One. It is understood that she is perceived as "Śrī" and as "Lakṣmī. ||16||
The Earth Goddess, the supporter and supported of the fourteen worlds beginning with Bhūr, consisting of the seven continents and the waters of the oceans, is of the nature of the Praṇava.
Blue in color and garlanded with lightning from her mouth, she assumes all forms for the sake of nourishing all medicinal herbs and all living beings. (8)
In the lower part of the entire universe, she consists of the nature of water and is composed of frogs; thus she is known as the Support of the World (bhuvanādhāra). ||19||
From the mouth of Hari, the Nāda arises, which is the very nature of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). From that Nāda comes the Bindu; from the Bindu, the Oṃkāra.
Beyond the syllable Oṃ is the Vaikhānasa mountain of Rāma;
on that mountain there are many branches consisting of both action and knowledge. (20)
Therein, the first scripture consists of the three Vedas and reveals all objects; it is celebrated as the "Trayī" because its nature comprises the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (21)
Established by their cause and their effects, they are proclaimed to be fourfold:
the Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, the Sāman chants, and likewise the Atharvāṅgirasa hymns.
Because the Cāturhotra is its primary element, the triad beginning with the Liṅga constitutes the Trayī;
the form of the Atharvāṅgirasa consists of the Sāman, Ṛk, and Yajus.
Likewise, they are taught individually according to the commonality of their ritual applications; thus, the Ṛgveda is proclaimed to have twenty-one branches. (24)
There are one hundred and nine births of the Yajus,
while the Sāman has a thousand branches, and the Atharvan has five branches.
At the beginning of that [age], the direct perception [of the Lord] was established according to the Vaikhānasa doctrine;
thereafter, the Vaikhānasa doctrine is constantly remembered by the sages. (26)
Grammar, exegesis, phonetics, etymology, astronomy, and prosody—these are the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga). ||27||
The Upāṅgas, the Āyana, the extensive Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya, and likewise the Vedaveda, which is further augmented for the sake of those who serve the knowledge of Dharma. ||28||
The Nibandhas, all the Śākhās, and the codification of traditional customs;
the Dharmaśāstra of the great sages, which is produced from their inner hearts;
and that which is known as Itihāsa and Purāṇa—these are proclaimed as the Upāṅgas. ||29||
O Sage, the Vāstuveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharvaveda, and Āyurveda—these five are proclaimed as the Upavedas. ||30||
Punishment, statesmanship, commerce, knowledge, and the supreme mastery over the vital breath—this self-luminous [system] is proclaimed to have twenty-one divisions. (31)
Formerly, the speech of Viṣṇu emerged from the Vaikhānasa Ṛṣi;
having conceived itself in the form of the three Vedas (Trayī), the embodied one thus manifests.
Having previously conceptualized it according to its numerical form as taught by the sage Vaikhānasa,
listen to me describe it in its entirety exactly as it was first revealed:
the eternal form consisting of Brahman is declared to be the power of action (kriyā-śakti).

The direct power (*sākṣācchakti*) of the Blessed One consists of manifestation and appearance through the mere act of remembrance; it takes the form of both restraint and grace, and the forms of tranquility and splendor. It possesses the various features of manifest and unmanifest causes, as well as distinct limbs, faces, and colors. Accompanying the Blessed One, inseparable from Him, and eternally co-residing with Him, she is called the "direct power" because of her capacity for all powers—such as creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace—through her manifest and unmanifest forms, and her opening and closing of the eyes. ||34||

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is threefold; in the state of dissolution, for the sake of resting, she rests upon the Lord’s right chest in the form of the *śrīvatsa*—this is the power of yoga (*yoga-śakti*). ||35||

The power of enjoyment, manifesting in the form of enjoyment, is supported by the nine treasures—such as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), the cow of plenty (*kāmadhenu*), the thought-gem (*cintāmaṇi*), the conch (*śaṅkha*), and the lotus-treasure (*padmanidhi*)—and it attends to the devotees of the Lord through their desires or even without desire. Whether through devotion accompanied by obligatory and occasional rites such as the *agnihotra*, or through the limbs of yoga—namely restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—or even with the slightest effort, whether by means of city gates, ramparts, celestial palaces (*vimāna*), and so forth, along with the implements for worshiping the image of the Lord’s form, such as bathing, anointing, and other festivals; [all these serve the devotee].
Everything is performed—whether through ancestral rites, offerings of food and drink, or other acts—after declaring that it is for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One. ||36||

Now, therefore, Vīraśakti has four arms, holding the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting as well as a lotus; she is adorned with a crown and ornaments, surrounded by all the gods, and is being consecrated at the foot of a Kalpa tree with jars of jewel-encrusted nectar-water by four elephants. She is being saluted by all the deities, beginning with Brahmā, endowed with the eight supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*, praised face-to-face by the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, lauded by the Vedas, Śāstras, and other scriptures, served by celestial nymphs such as Jayā and others, and illuminated by the two lamps of the Sun and the Moon.

Being sung of by Tumburu, Nārada, and others; being shaded by Rākā and Sinīvālī with a parasol; being fanned by Hlādinī and Māyā with chowries; being worshipped by Svāhā, Svadhā, Bhṛgu, Puṇya, and others; the Goddess Lakṣmī, seated upon a lotus on a divine throne, the performer of all causes and effects—her separate manifestation from the Lord is conceived as such.
Steadfast and with gracious eyes, she adorned [the Lord] while being worshipped by all the deities; she is known as Vīralakṣmī. Thus ends the Upaniṣad. 37.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, O Holy Ones. With firm limbs and bodies, may we praise you.
May we attain the life-span ordained by the gods. May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being;
may Pūṣan, the knower of all things, grant us well-being.
May Tārkṣya, with his uninjured wheel, grant us well-being;
may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
